newsitem.title: UK: Cyberspace spawns new scam - Internet hijackings.
newsitem.headline: Cyberspace spawns new scam - Internet hijackings.

text.p: As more and more companies enter the world of cyberspace, they all too often find themselves victims of a new scam: Internet hijacking.

The victims are companies that have failed to register their own names, or the brand names of their products, as Internet addresses, only to find that a third party has appropriated their name for a Web site. In such cases, companies either must pay the third party for the use of their own name or take legal action to win back the right.

High-profile victims of Internet hijackings have included Harrods, the luxury London department store, which last month went to court to reclaim the Internet address http://www.harrods.com, fast-food chain operator McDonald's and music television station MTV.

Those cases and others are causing Internet experts to warn companies that they must register brand names on the Internet as automatically as they register new trademarks in order to protect against hijackings in cyberspace.

"This country has 30,000 new brands every single day," Ajaz Ahmed, managing partner of AKQA, a London-based new media agency, told Reuters. "If a new brand is announced people need to ensure that the (Internet) domain name is reserved for that brand name. It's just like making sure you have a registered trademark.
"The risk is that someone else will register that name, and the brand name owner will have to pay to use that name," Ahmed added.

Establishing Web sites on the Internet is becoming an increasingly common practice among companies, many of whom are just beginning to tap into the marketing potential of the Internet. The tens of thousands of Web sites on the Internet, an international computer network, include vast ranges of consumer products, such as cars, spirits and electronics.

But the global reach of the Internet, a network of computers that allow users to tap into Web sites around the world, has made it almost a virtual Wild West. The regulations that do exist are strictly national, but the global aspects of the medium mean that continual questions arise over jurisdiction.

When Harrods last year discovered that a man named Michael Lawrie and four associates had registered the Internet address harrods.com, it filed suit in Britain, where a High Court judge last month ruled that the registration "clearly constituted infringement of Harrods' registered trademarks and passing off."
The ruling, however, set no clear legal precedent in Britain because the defendants failed to appear in court and, as a result, the judge did not have to give a detailed ruling on the case.
The harrods.com Internet address, however, had been registered in the United States.

"The UK court in the Harrods case actually ordered the guys to give up the name," noted Ivan Pope, chief executive officer of NetNames, the leading UK Internet domain name registry. "But the UK court would have no power over the registry. It seems to me ... that Harrods should have gone to law in the U.S."
Other Internet hijacking victims have chosen to simply settle out of court by paying a fee to win back the right to their brand name as an Internet address.

McDonald's, the U.S.-based fast-food restaurant operator, settled out of court to win back the rights to the Internet address http://www.mcdonalds.com after an American journalist registered the name.
Although a company may carry a trademark on a brand name, the trademark gives it no automatic right to use the name as an Internet address.
"It is still first come, first served, so anyone can register any name," Pope said. "The best way to protect your brand names is to register them before someone else does."
Registering an Internet address is quick and cheap.
"It costs less than $150 and it takes less than five minutes," said AKQA's Ahmed.

The registration process and the cost does vary, however, on a country by country basis. "There are different requirements all over the world," said Pope. "Some countries have no requirements. Some fees are high, like Japan."

There is a move underway to establish an international body that would handle all Internet name registrations. The Internet Ad Hoc Committee, which also represents the International Telecommunications Union and the World Intellectual Property Organisation, is proposing new categories for Internet addresses and is also proposing establishing an international body based in Switzerland to oversee Internet registrations and issues.
